title: How to access occupational therapy | NHS inform
text:
How to access occupational therapy
How you access occupational therapy depends on your condition and where you live.
Short-term conditions
A short-term condition is likely to improve with time. For example, after you’ve recovered from an operation.
Speak to your healthcare professionals if you have a short-term condition. They’ll discuss if you can be referred for occupational therapy.
If you do need occupational therapy, you’ll have an assessment. Your occupational therapist will then discuss if you need any equipment or rehabilitation.
Equipment or rehabilitation may be provided for free by the NHS. However, this can depend on what’s available from your local health board and Social Care Partnership (HSCP).
Long-term conditions
A long-term condition isn’t likely to improve with time. For example, if you have a permanent disability.
A long-term condition can affect your ability to carry out everyday activities. If this is the case, you may be able to access occupational therapy through your local Health and Social Care Partnership (HSCP). They may work with local NHS providers, local authorities and other organisations.
You can contact your local authority for an occupational therapy assessment. You can also be referred for an assessment by:
your GP
a consultant (specialist doctor)
a nurse
another healthcare professional
a social care professional
You can
search for your local authority
on the
GOV.UK
website.
Eligibility criteria
Local authorities have eligibility criteria. They use this to decide if someone can receive social care services like occupational therapy.
The criteria is based on legislation called the
Care and Support (Eligibility Criteria) Regulations 2014
.
Each local authority may have slightly different criteria. However, all should include the following points:
You need help because you have a physical or mental impairment or illness.
You’re unable to carry out necessary tasks as a result of this impairment or illness. For example, washing yourself, getting dressed or going to the toilet.
You’re unable to complete these tasks which has a negative impact on your health and wellbeing.
Private occupational therapy
You can contact an occupational therapist directly. You may do this if you don’t want to access occupational therapy through the NHS or your local authority.
If you decide to see a private occupational therapist, make sure they’re fully qualified. They should be a member of a recognised body. For example, the
Royal College of Occupational Therapists (RCOT)
.
Only healthcare professionals registered with the
Health and Care Professions Council (HCPC)
are allowed to use the title of occupational therapist.
You can see if your occupational therapist is registered on the
HCPC online register
.
Source:
Royal College of Occupational Therapists
